name: Adam Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 58, lead developer at a tech company that runs arena ticket gates. I have a master's degree and a good wage, but I still use the steward's signed count when a scanner freezes; I have never used AI tools. My partner works full-time in medical records, our sons are grown, and we own our home outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the stewards that a ticket scan should not open a gate after the crowd limit is reached. I lead software for a tech company's arena-entry system and have never used AI; I check the turnstile count against the steward's signed sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI makes only small changes, I expect my lead job and our wages to stay sound. I have a master's degree and high pay, my partner works full-time in medical records, our home is paid off, and eleven months of expenses are saved; many software firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking duplicate-scan bugs against the steward count sheet. We'd save another 170 monthly while both wages hold, because our retirement figures are still unchecked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and money. I still do not like a green gate light when the concourse is already full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the steward count show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fan scanned the same ticket twice after the reader froze. The screen counted two entrants, but the steward counted one, so I corrected the tally before the next gate opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown sons live in other places and pay their own bills. They come to a match with us, not to fund our retirement.

I'd keep **crowd limits** ahead of a green turnstile light.
think: I expect **two wages** and my lead post to hold under mild AI.
I have **eleven months saved** and a paid-off home.
do: Keep **correcting duplicate scans** against signed steward counts.

feel: **Calm** about present income, alert to crowded gates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write ticket code and answer fans quickly, but the steward must be able to hold a gate when the concourse is full. I would not accept a faster queue that hides a bad count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role could lose hours if the firm reduces the people checking routine scans. Eleven months saved and my partner's wage protect us for a while, but losing my larger pay would change when I can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep an exception list of duplicate scans for the weekly venue review and ask the arena manager for a written paid staffing plan. We'd defer replacing our kitchen cabinets until the firm settles hours; I'd consider a paid gate-audit role only if actually posted with signed wages that with my partner's cover food, health and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post, though we are not short of next month's bills. I want the steward to have a real stop button, not an apology form after people are hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the count trustworthy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The duplicate scan must be compared with a count from a steward standing at that gate. The dashboard should not be allowed to invent a second person in the concourse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why can the cabinets wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our cabinets close properly; the finish is worn, not dangerous. My partner and I would keep that money liquid until our paid hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write gate code before entrance robots arrive around 2031. A steward must still be able to stop entry when a count is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead post quickly if software writes and checks ticket scans. My partner's medical-records wage covers our basic bills, and eleven months saved buys search time, but I have no verified pension amount to replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask four nearby firms and the arena operator for actual paid gate-safety or software-test vacancies, wages and start dates. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's covers food, health and travel without an unpaid health-cover gap; if none qualifies, I'd seek available paid local work while using savings and check insurance dates before cover ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage at 60. Eleven months saved buys interviews, not a retirement cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show another firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show another employer the anonymised double-scan case and the steward's corrected count. It explains why the concourse was not as full as the screen claimed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What dates would your partner check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare start dates and medical cover. A delayed first payslip could eat into savings even if the annual salary looked good.

I'd check **actual paid vacancies** before claiming a fallback.
think: I expect **my lead post** could be cut fast.
I cannot count **an unknown pension** as replacement wages.

A long cushion buys **search time**, while signed wages and continuous health cover remain necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives time to check whether retirement at 63 is affordable before thinking AI reaches gate code. Entrance robots follow around 2034, but my software work changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could bring retirement forward if the verified figures work, but I will not use a paid-off home or eleven months saved as a made-up pension. My partner's medical-records wage is part of the calculation only while it is actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking arena release counts while we request both retirement statements and price health cover after my employer's plan ends. If verified retirement income plus my partner's actual wage covers food, health and travel, and my partner agrees, I'd retire at 63; otherwise in the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid work if offered or apply to signed local jobs covering those bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious until the amounts are on paper, though I like having five years to check. A retirement date is not a health-insurance card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figures must you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The statements need monthly amounts and start dates, and the health quote must be for both of us. We cannot use today's employee premium after my wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who agrees before you resign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would decide together because my leaving work changes the household insurance and travel. If the medical-records wage changes, we'd recalculate before I hand in notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might put me at 68, but thinking AI would reach ticket code before entrance robots around 2039. I want a steward's count to remain part of a safe release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages, paid-off home and eleven-month reserve make bills secure. I have not verified a retirement amount, and I cannot assume the arena will still pay for my software work at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the double-scan test and save 170 monthly while both wages hold, then check both retirement statements and future health premiums each year. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified income covers food, health and travel; otherwise I'd keep an available paid role or seek real local work without counting our sons' wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work, but current money is steady. I would rather leave a correct gate count than a claim that a green dashboard never fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the test preserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should show one fan, two scans and the steward's corrected count. A later developer can see why we did not close the turnstile on a number alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons pay retirement costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sons have their own households. They can join us for a match, but they do not owe us retirement pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could remove lead gate-code work before another employer pays me to check safety. Written notice, real vacancies with health cover and time to check insurance dates would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who stands at a gate when the count is wrong. The steward can see a person, not a database row; I want that judgment to have a stop button.

headlineQuote: The steward can see a person, not a database row; I want that judgment to have a stop button.
portrait: Adam, **58**, leads arena-entry software after a master's degree and checks duplicate scans against signed steward counts.
His **higher wage**, partner's medical-records pay, paid-off home, eleven-month reserve and many local firms secure current bills.
He has **never used AI** and insists a steward can hold a gate when the software's crowd count is wrong.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; signed replacement work must cover household bills and uninterrupted health cover.
At 63 he considers **early retirement** only with verified pension amounts, actual partner wages, new health premiums and joint agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his larger wage before a paid arena-safety job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid vacancies and continuous health cover would help him plan.
